_about: Object catalog for Ashcombe Meadow (plan 10 §4.1, v3). One entry per inspectable thing in the main scene, built from the owner-approved S0 draft (repos/immersive/_direction/field-ecologist/objects.draft.json, 2026-10-30) with every draft note resolved. Fields: id, name, short (<= 25 words), more (<= 120 words), whyItMatters (learning objective, or empty for pure exploration), realSize (metres, 1 unit = 1 m), honesty (real / reconstructed / fictional / illustrative / time-lapse), source (a URL listed in research/sources.md, or research/meadow-model-notes.md for things this project made up), role (task / explore). The meadow, its five species and the station are fictional teaching models. realSizeBasis says what each realSize measures; the assets behind each entry are mapped in public/assets/v3/manifest.json (catalog ids). Checked by scripts/check-v3-assets.mjs.

realSizeBasis.butterweed: Procedural model bounds (src/systems/species-models.js): 52 cm tall, inside the 40-55 cm in content/species.json
realSizeBasis.daisyleaf: Procedural model bounds: 11 cm tall rosette, inside 8-15 cm
realSizeBasis.blue-sedge: Procedural model bounds: 44 cm tall, arching blades spread about 70 cm, inside 30-45 cm
realSizeBasis.bunchgrass: Procedural model bounds: 35 cm tall, inside 25-35 cm
realSizeBasis.fen-orchid: Procedural model bounds: 26 cm tall, inside 20-30 cm
realSizeBasis.quadrat: One 2 m x 2 m frame of 3 cm bars (content/species.json quadratSizeM)
realSizeBasis.random-sampling: One survey stake (own model): 0.6 m tall including the 6 cm point, tape included
realSizeBasis.field-station: The station table (Poly Haven wooden_table_02 bounds); the guide, flask, pencils and stool are parts of the station but the table carries the id
realSizeBasis.soil: The cut stream bank where the topsoil shows: 3 m long, 0.4 m deep, 0.4 m into the bank
realSizeBasis.hills: Hill ring around the meadow: outer diameter 680 m, crest up to about 56 m
realSizeBasis.fallen-log: Poly Haven dead_tree_trunk bounds at real scale (v2 scaled it up; v3 does not)
realSizeBasis.margin-flowers: One clump (Poly Haven periwinkle_plant_01); the margin has many clumps of periwinkle, gazania and celandine
realSizeBasis.mist: One mist bank: 26 m x 20 m sheets stacked about 2 m deep
realSizeBasis.sun-dawn: True solar diameter at the true Earth-Sun distance (realDistance): the scale check compares the angular size the camera sees, about 0.53 degrees
realSizeBasis.clouds: A typical small cumulus cloud, about 1 km across
realSizeBasis.butterflies: Wingspan x body depth x body length of a meadow butterfly
realSizeBasis.bees: Body length x height x width of a bee
realSizeBasis.birds: Wingspan x height x body length of a small bird in flight
realSizeBasis.field-worker: Adult figure: shoulder width x height x depth

objects.name: Meadow Butterweed
objects.short: Knee-high single stems with one round yellow head on a bare stalk. It grows in dense patches.
objects.more: Field marks: an upright single stem 40 to 55 cm tall, alternate lance-shaped toothed leaves, and one round yellow head 2 to 3 cm across. Colour is only a secondary cue, so confirm with shape and height. It grows in clumps, so where you put a quadrat changes the count a lot. This is a fictional teaching species.
objects.whyItMatters: The research-question species: its clumping is why random placement matters.

objects.name: Common Daisy-leaf
objects.short: A flat rosette of round, toothed leaves at hand height, with one or two tiny white button flowers.
objects.more: Field marks: all the leaves spread from one point at ground level. The flowers are under 1.5 cm across, on short stalks with no leaves. It is scattered at random across the meadow. Young Bunchgrass also sits low, but its blades are narrow and folded. This is a fictional teaching species.
objects.whyItMatters: Background herb: shows what a random distribution looks like.

objects.name: Blue Sedge
objects.short: Dense blue-green tufts whose blades arch out from the base. It grows thicker the wetter the ground.
objects.more: Field marks: tufts 30 to 45 cm tall, blades arching out from the base, and no yellow head. It grows more densely where the soil is wetter, so it is thicker near the stream. That gradient is why stratified sampling helps. This is a fictional teaching species.

objects.name: Tussock Bunchgrass
objects.short: Tight, upright grass tussocks that cover much of the meadow.
objects.more: Field marks: tussocks 25 to 35 cm tall with narrow, folded blades. It is common and evenly scattered. Counting it is slow because there are so many, which is a good reason to use small quadrats. This is a fictional teaching species.
objects.whyItMatters: Dense random species: quadrat size and effort.

objects.name: Fen Orchid
objects.short: Slender single stems in a few small colonies. It is rare, so most quadrats will contain none.
objects.more: Field marks: slender stems 20 to 30 cm tall in small groups, topped by a loose spike of tiny greenish flowers. Because it is rare and clumped, a few quadrats can miss it entirely, or hit a colony and overestimate it. This is a fictional teaching species.
objects.whyItMatters: Rare species: shows the limits of a small sample.

objects.name: Quadrat frame (2 m × 2 m)
objects.short: A square frame laid on the ground. You count every plant of a species whose base is inside it.
objects.more: Ecologists use quadrats to estimate how many plants grow in an area. Several quadrats at random places give a fair sample. The average count per quadrat, scaled up to the whole field, gives the estimate. The right quadrat size depends on the organism. Here each frame is 2 m on a side in a 100 m field.
objects.whyItMatters: The core sampling tool of the case.

objects.name: Clipboard and data sheet
objects.short: Your data sheet. Each count you record is written here, quadrat by quadrat.
objects.more: The sheet lists each quadrat's number, position, species and count. Writing every count down as you go means the sample can be checked and analysed later. The sheet fills as you count, and it feeds the population estimate in Module 4.
objects.whyItMatters: Modules 3 and 4: the data you analyse.

objects.name: Hand lens (magnifier)
objects.short: A magnifier on the station table. Use it to look closely at leaves, flower heads and stems before you count.
objects.more: Look-alike plants differ in small details: leaf shape, the teeth on the leaf edge, and where the leaves join the stem. The close-up view shows these field marks clearly, so you can confirm a species before you count it. The five species are fictional teaching models.

objects.name: Numbered survey stakes
objects.short: Numbered stakes with pink tape mark where the random draw put each quadrat. Nobody chose these spots by eye.
objects.more: In simple random sampling, every spot has the same chance of being picked. If you pick spots by eye, you tend to choose showy patches, and that biases the estimate. Each stake marks one drawn spot. Its number matches a row on your data sheet.

objects.name: Field station table
objects.short: A wooden table by the gate with the field guide, a flask and pencils, and a folding stool beside it.
objects.more: The survey starts here, and you come back here between modules. The field guide on the table lists the five teaching species and their field marks. Open it at any time to check a plant.

objects.name: Stream
objects.short: A shallow stream along the west side of the meadow. The ground gets wetter the closer you get to it.
objects.more: Water flowing past the field keeps the nearby soil damp. Plants that like wet ground, such as Blue Sedge here, grow more densely close to it. Inside the sampling area the stream line is damp ground, so no counted plant is ever under water. The water flows at a real-time pace.
objects.realSizeNote: A line, not an object: the channel is 1.9 m wide and 0.3 m deep along a 220 m course (z -60 to 160 m), and it follows the ground, so its bounding box measures the terrain it crosses.

objects.name: Wet ground
objects.short: Darker, lusher ground near the stream, where Blue Sedge grows thickest.
objects.more: Soil moisture changes across the meadow. If you split the field into wet and dry strata and sample each one separately, you get a better estimate when a species follows that gradient. This strip is the streamside stratum.
objects.realSizeNote: A stratum (a layer of ground), not an object: x 0 to 33.3 m by z 0 to 100 m, sward 0.3 m deep. The clickable patch by the stream is one part of it.

objects.name: Dry ground
objects.short: Paler, firmer ground on the higher east side of the field, away from the stream.
objects.more: This is the drier stratum. Compare how often Blue Sedge appears here and near the stream.
objects.realSizeNote: A stratum (a layer of ground), not an object: x 66.7 to 100 m by z 0 to 100 m, sward 0.3 m deep. The clickable patch on the rise is one part of it.

objects.name: Soil
objects.short: Dark topsoil with roots and small stones, seen where the stream has cut into its bank.
objects.more: Topsoil is the dark top layer of the soil. It is rich in humus, the decaying remains of plants and animals, which helps the soil hold water and gives plants minerals. How much water the soil holds is the main thing that changes across this meadow.

objects.name: Hedgerow
objects.short: A line of shrubs and small trees along the north boundary, outside the sampling area.
objects.more: A hedgerow is a line of bushes that marks a boundary. It often has trees in it. Many birds nest in hedgerows in spring and summer. This one is background dressing and is never counted. Its shrubs are this project's own models, with leaf and bark textures from ambientCG. The nettles and undergrowth are Poly Haven scans.
objects.realSizeNote: A line: 110 m long (x -6 to 104 m), shrubs 2.9 m tall and 3.1 m deep (own-work hedge-shrub LOD0). It follows the ground, so its bounding box also measures the slope it crosses.

objects.name: Woodland edge
objects.short: Broadleaf woodland beyond the hedgerow. It is scenery, not part of the survey.
objects.more: The trees are generic broadleaf models made for this project, not a particular species. Trees far away are drawn as flat picture cards, called impostors, so the scene stays fast. A stump and fallen branches lie on the woodland floor, where decaying wood is home to fungi and beetle larvae.
objects.realSizeNote: An area: a woodland block about 150 m by 40 m, trees up to 15.9 m tall (own-work tree-tall LOD0), on rising ground.

objects.name: Distant hills
objects.short: Low, rolling hills on the horizon, softened by the morning haze.
objects.more: The air between you and the hills scatters sunlight, so the far hills look paler and hazier than the near ones. The hills are scenery for the fictional meadow.

objects.name: Dry-stone wall and gate
objects.short: A wall of stones stacked without mortar along the south side, with a five-bar gate by the field station.
objects.more: A dry-stone wall is made only of stones fitted carefully together, with no mortar to glue them. Such walls are easy to repair one section at a time. This one marks the south boundary of the fictional field.
objects.realSizeNote: A line: 128 m long (x -14 to 114 m), 1.1 m high and 0.55 m wide. It follows the ground, so its bounding box also measures the slope it crosses.

objects.name: Fallen log
objects.short: A decaying trunk beyond the east boundary, a home for fungi and beetles.
objects.more: Dead and decaying wood gives fungi a place to feed and beetle larvae a place to grow, and birds come to eat the insects. As it rots, it slowly returns its nutrients to the ground. This log is a free (CC0) Poly Haven scan placed outside the field.

objects.name: Margin flowers
objects.short: Pink, orange and small yellow flowers along the wall and hedge foot, outside the field. They are not part of the survey.
objects.more: These are free (CC0) Poly Haven plant scans used as scenery. They grow only outside the sampling area, and they were chosen so they cannot be mistaken for the five counted species. Bees and butterflies visit them.

objects.name: Morning mist
objects.short: Low mist over the stream that drifts and thins as the Sun warms the ground.
objects.more: On clear, calm nights the ground cools and chills the air just above it. Water vapour then condenses into tiny droplets, most readily near rivers and wet ground. The mist usually clears soon after sunrise as the ground warms. The rate shown here is time-lapse.

objects.name: Rising Sun
objects.short: The Sun rises over the hills. The app speeds it up so you can see the light change.
objects.more: When the Sun is low, its light passes through more air. The air scatters away more of the blue, so morning light looks warm and yellow, and shadows are long. The sunrise speed is time-lapse, and calm mode holds it still while you count.

objects.name: Clouds and cloud shadows
objects.short: Clouds drift across the sky, and their shadows slide over the meadow.
objects.more: In this scene the clouds drift with the wind, and their shadows sweep across the ground below them. The drift speed and the cloud shapes are illustrative.

objects.name: Butterflies
objects.short: Butterflies visit the flowers along the margins. They fly in short, fluttering hops.
objects.more: Butterflies drink nectar from flowers. As they land, pollen sticks to their bodies and is carried to the next flower, which pollinates it. They fly over the margins only, never over quadrats, so they do not get in the way while you count. Their flight paths are illustrative.

objects.name: Bees
objects.short: Bees work the flower heads along the margins, moving from one flower to the next.
objects.more: Bees collect pollen on purpose, and they drink nectar too. Moving from flower to flower, they carry pollen between plants and pollinate many meadow flowers. Their paths here are illustrative.

objects.name: Birds overhead
objects.short: Small birds fly across the meadow between the hedgerow and the woodland.
objects.more: Many birds nest in hedgerows in spring and summer, and they feed in the fields and woods nearby. These birds are illustrative, and so are their flight paths.

objects.name: Field worker in the distance
objects.short: Another ecologist is laying out a long tape at the far side of the meadow.
objects.more: This worker is a fictional colleague setting out a tape line for another part of the survey. They never touch your quadrats or your sample.

objects.name: Wind in the grass
objects.short: Gusts roll across the meadow as waves of bending grass.
objects.more: In this scene each gust bends the grass as it passes, so waves travel across the field with the wind. The motion is illustrative, and it pauses in calm mode while you count.
objects.realSizeNote: A motion of the sward, not an object: it moves the 100 m x 100 m meadow and the long grass at its margins.
